# aeneid-047 — new house renderings

No new house renderings. No set piece on the pending list falls in VI.703–800 (VI.851–853 is in the next part).

For the reviewer (not proposed as house renderings), the best-known lines of the part, built from the Latin alone:

- VI.726–727 *totamque infusa per artus / mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet.*
  - `l`: "a breath within nourishes, and, poured through the limbs, / mind drives the whole bulk and with the great body mixes itself."
  - `i`: "…draw their nourishment from a spirit inside them, and a mind, poured into every limb, keeps the whole bulk astir and blends itself with that vast body."
  - Avoided the "mind moves the mass" / "mingles with the mighty mass" shapes; "bulk" for *molem*, "blends" in `i`. Reviewer: "are fed by a spirit within… a mind spread through all their members" ran close to a known version and was rephrased.
- VI.743 *quisque suos patimur Manes*
  - `l`: "each we suffer our own Manes;"
  - `i`: "every one of us endures the ghostly lot that is his own;"
  - `l` is the bare literal; `i` avoids the familiar "each of us must suffer his own ghost / shade / Manes" formulas (reviewer moved it further from the "each of us suffers…" shape).
- VI.776 *Haec tum nomina erunt, nunc sunt sine nomine terrae.*
  - `l`: "These then will be names; now they are lands without a name."
  - `i`: "In that age these will be famous names; today they are stretches of country that no one has named."
  - `l` is close to word-for-word and cannot avoid resembling other literal versions; `i` avoids the common "nameless lands" / "places without names" endings.
- VI.791–797 *Hic vir, hic est… stellis ardentibus aptum.*
  - `l`: "This man, this is he, whom you hear promised to you rather often, / Augustus Caesar, offspring of the Deified, who golden will found / ages once more in Latium, through the fields ruled / by Saturn of old, and beyond both Garamantes and Indians / will push forward the empire: lies outside the stars a land, / outside the paths of the year and of the sun, where sky-bearing Atlas / the axis on his shoulder turns, fitted with burning stars."
  - `i`: "This is the man, yes, this is he, whom you hear pledged to you again and again: Augustus Caesar, offspring of a god, who will found anew in Latium an age of gold, across the countryside that Saturn ruled in times long past, and push the bounds of empire beyond the Garamantes and the Indians: there is a country lying beyond the constellations, beyond the roads of the year and of the sun, where Atlas the sky-bearer turns on his shoulder the axle of heaven, studded with blazing stars."
  - Avoided "This, this is he, whom thou so oft hast heard" (Dryden's shape) and "so often promised"; avoided "bring back the age of gold" / "golden age again" phrasing in favour of "establish an age of gold"; avoided "a land beyond the stars" word order in `i`. Line 797 repeats 4.482. Reviewer: `l` 797 already matched aeneid-028 word for word; the end of `i` now follows aeneid-028 ("turns on his shoulder the axle of heaven, studded with blazing stars"). "promised to you so many times", "son of a god" and "the fields where Saturn reigned" were close to known versions and were rephrased.
- Reviewer, other lines rephrased for remembered English (see review.md): 703–705, 707–709, 713–715, 719–723, 728–742, 744–766, 767–772, 777–779, 781–790, 798–800.
